# SentinelPay — Threat Model & Register (D-01)

**Status:** Draft from Cycle 1 code walkthrough, based on direct review of `payments-api` and `kyc-api` source. Confirm this against your team's call notes and update as Cycle 2 remediation lands.

**Note on how this was built:** rather than guessing at threats abstractly, this register is grounded in real code found in `Amdari-Project--02/services/`. Every entry below traces to a specific file and, where the codebase authors left one, a specific `V-ID` comment. This is stronger evidence than a purely theoretical threat model, use it as your working draft and adjust wording/severity based on what your team actually discussed on the call.

---

## Architecture & Trust Boundaries

The diagram below shows how the two services connect to each other, the database, and the outside world. **The dashed red lines are the trust boundaries**, every point where an arrow crosses one of these lines is a point where data moves from a more-trusted context into a less-trusted one, and that's exactly where the threats in the register below are concentrated.

![SentinelPay architecture and trust boundary diagram](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two boundaries are marked:

1. **Internet → Application** — where `User / merchant` requests reach `payments-api` and `kyc-api`. Anything crossing this line is fully untrusted until the application authenticates and authorises it. This is where the identity-related threats (T-01, T-02, T-03, T-08, T-09) concentrate.
2. **Application → Data / External** — where the two services reach out to PostgreSQL, S3, and the two external endpoints (the merchant webhook and the BVN provider). This boundary runs in *both* directions: inbound (what the app sends to the database can be malicious, T-04/T-05) and outbound (what the app fetches from an external URL can be abused, T-10/T-11).

Not shown for simplicity: Redis (session/idempotency cache) and the CI/CD pipeline's connection into AWS, both are covered separately once the Cloud and DevSecOps tracks produce their own architecture.

---

## Trust Boundary Map

| ID | Boundary | Description |
|---|---|---|
| TB-01 | User/Merchant → `payments-api` | All login, account, transaction, wallet, webhook, and admin endpoints |
| TB-02 | User/Merchant → `kyc-api` | BVN/NIN verification and document upload/retrieval |
| TB-03 | `payments-api` → PostgreSQL | Account, transaction, user, webhook tables |
| TB-04 | `kyc-api` → PostgreSQL | KYC records table |
| TB-05 | `payments-api` → external webhook URL | Merchant-supplied callback URL, fetched server-side |
| TB-06 | `kyc-api` → external BVN provider URL | Merchant-suppliable provider URL, fetched server-side |
| TB-07 | `kyc-api` → S3 (document storage) | KYC document upload/retrieval via boto3 |
| TB-08 | `payments-api` internal → admin endpoints | Same ALB as public endpoints, no network separation |

## Threat Register

| ID | Boundary | STRIDE | Threat Description | Evidence | Likelihood | Impact | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-01 | TB-01 | Spoofing | JWT verification calls `verify_signature: False`, so any caller can forge a token for any user or role without knowing the secret | `payments-api/app/auth.py`, `decode_token()` — tagged V-APP-02 (part 2) | High | Critical | Open |
| T-02 | TB-01 | Spoofing | JWT is signed with HS256 using a hardcoded fallback secret (`"sentinelpay-dev-secret"`) committed in source | `payments-api/app/auth.py`, `payments-api/app/main.py`, `kyc-api/app/auth.py` — tagged V-APP-02 (part 1) | High | Critical | Open |
| T-03 | TB-01 | Info Disclosure | Account lookup endpoint returns any account by ID with no ownership check | `payments-api/app/routes/accounts.py`, `get_account()` — tagged V-APP-03, this is the originating incident | High | Critical | Open |
| T-04 | TB-01, TB-03 | Tampering | Transaction search concatenates the `q` and `account_id` parameters directly into SQL | `payments-api/app/routes/transactions.py`, `search_transactions()` — tagged V-APP-01 | High | Critical | Open |
| T-05 | TB-02, TB-04 | Tampering | KYC lookup by BVN/NIN concatenates input directly into SQL | `kyc-api/app/routes/verify.py`, `lookup_kyc()` — same root cause as V-APP-01 | High | Critical | Open |
| T-06 | TB-01 | Tampering | Wallet debit reads and writes balance with no row lock or transaction boundary; two concurrent debits can both succeed against the same pre-balance | `payments-api/app/routes/wallets.py`, `debit_wallet()` — tagged V-APP-05 | Medium | High | Open |
| T-07 | TB-01 | Tampering / Elevation | Profile update endpoint writes every key-value pair the client sends, including `status`, `user_id`, and `balance` | `payments-api/app/routes/accounts.py`, `update_profile()` — tagged V-APP-07 | Medium | Critical | Open |
| T-08 | TB-01 | Elevation | Registration endpoint lets the client self-assign `role` (e.g. request `role: admin` directly) | `payments-api/app/routes/auth.py`, `register()` — tagged V-APP-07 variant | Medium | Critical | Open |
| T-09 | TB-01, TB-08 | Elevation | Admin-only check trusts the JWT's `role` claim with no server-side verification against the database; combined with T-01/T-02, any caller can self-promote to admin | `payments-api/app/routes/admin.py`, `list_users()` — tagged V-APP-03 variant | High | Critical | Open |
| T-10 | TB-05 | Tampering / Info Disclosure | Webhook test endpoint fetches any attacker-supplied URL with no allowlist, scheme check, or IP filter (SSRF, including cloud metadata endpoint access) | `payments-api/app/routes/webhooks.py`, `test_webhook()` — tagged V-APP-04 | Medium | High | Open |
| T-11 | TB-06 | Tampering / Info Disclosure | BVN verification lets the caller override the provider URL entirely, same SSRF pattern as T-10 | `kyc-api/app/routes/verify.py`, `verify_bvn()` | Medium | High | Open |
| T-12 | TB-01 | Spoofing | Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5, trivially reversible via rainbow tables | `payments-api/app/auth.py`, `hash_password()` — tagged V-APP-06 | Medium | High | Open |
| T-13 | TB-01 | DoS | Login, registration, and OTP endpoints have no rate limiting; brute force and email enumeration are trivial | `payments-api/app/routes/auth.py`, all three endpoints — tagged V-APP-08 | Medium | Medium | Open |
| T-14 | TB-01 | Info Disclosure | OTP codes are printed to application logs in plaintext | `payments-api/app/routes/auth.py`, `request_otp()` | Low | Medium | Open |
| T-15 | TB-08 | Elevation | Admin session restore deserialises a base64-encoded pickle blob with `pickle.loads`, allowing arbitrary code execution for any caller who can forge a token | `payments-api/app/routes/admin.py`, `restore_session()` — tagged V-APP-10 | Medium | Critical | Open |
| T-16 | TB-01 | Repudiation | Wallet debits (the most sensitive operation in the platform) have no structured audit log — who, what, when, from where | `payments-api/app/routes/wallets.py`, `debit_wallet()` — tagged V-APP-11 | Medium | Medium | Open |
| T-17 | TB-01, TB-02 | Info Disclosure | Unhandled exceptions return full stack traces in the JSON response body | `payments-api/app/main.py`, `handle_exception()` — tagged V-APP-09 | High | Medium | Open |
| T-18 | TB-01, TB-02 | Info Disclosure / Tampering | Both services run with `debug=True` hardcoded, exposing the interactive Werkzeug debugger in production-labeled environments | `payments-api/app/main.py`, `kyc-api/app/main.py` | Medium | High | Open |
| T-19 | TB-07 | Info Disclosure | KYC document uploads are stored with a public-read ACL and no filename sanitisation (path traversal possible) | `kyc-api/app/routes/documents.py`, `upload_document()` | High | Critical | Open |
| T-20 | TB-07 | Info Disclosure | Document retrieval has no ownership check on the storage key, any authenticated user can fetch any other user's KYC document if they know or guess the key | `kyc-api/app/routes/documents.py`, `get_document()` — same pattern as V-APP-03 | High | Critical | Open |
| T-21 | TB-03, TB-04 | Info Disclosure | Database credentials have a hardcoded fallback (`sentinel:sentinel123`) in `payments-api`, and `kyc-api`'s connection string comes from an unvalidated env var with no fallback check | `payments-api/app/db.py`, `kyc-api/app/db.py` | Medium | High | Open |

## Notes for the team

- **This list is not exhaustive.** It covers what's visible in the application code read during Cycle 1. Cloud-layer threats (V-CLD) and pipeline-layer threats (V-PIP) aren't in this register yet since they depend on Terraform and CI/CD work Femi, Ben, and Mohammed haven't started yet, add those as separate sections once that work begins.
- **T-09, T-15, and several others compound on top of T-01/T-02.** Worth discussing as a team whether fixing JWT validation first (before anything else) closes off the easiest path to several other findings at once, this is a real prioritisation question for Cycle 2.
- **Update the Status column as fixes land.** Change `Open` to `Mitigated` and add the commit/PR reference once Chinanza closes each item, don't leave this table static after today.
- **Add anything your team raised on the call that isn't captured here.** This was built from code alone; if the STRIDE conversation surfaced something not tied to a specific line of code (e.g. a process gap, a missing policy), add it as its own row even without a code reference.

## Register Update Log (Task 5: keeping this living)

This is what makes the register a living document instead of a one-time write-up. **Every time a threat's status changes, add a row here, don't just silently edit the table above.** This gives you a visible history of when and why each threat closed, which is itself evidence for D-02 (the remediation report references this same trail).

**The process, in three steps, every time something changes:**
1. Whoever merges the fixing PR updates the Status column in the Threat Register table above (`Open` → `Mitigated`, or `Open` → `Accepted Risk` with a reason).
2. They add one row to the log table below: date, threat ID, what changed, and a link to the PR/commit.
3. At each cycle review meeting, scan this log out loud as part of the agenda, this is how the team stays in sync on what's actually closed versus what's still assumed closed.

| Date | Threat ID(s) | Change | Linked PR / Commit | Updated by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| _(example)_ 2026-09-05 | T-01, T-02 | Marked Open → Mitigated: JWT now verifies signature, RS256 with rotated keys | PR #12 | Chinanza |

Delete the example row once real entries start landing.

**Ownership:** this log is not solely the Team Lead's job to maintain. Whoever closes a threat updates it as part of closing the PR, that's part of the Definition of Done for any fix touching a row in this register.
